hints: Count the longest continuous carbon chain in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}$ and identify which carbon carries the Br atom.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain**
Look at the formula $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}$. Count straight through, you have 4 carbons in a row, so the parent alkane is butane.

Number to give Br the lowest locant**
The Br is on the second carbon from either end here, so it is carbon 2. Put the substituent first alphabetically as bromo, giving $\text{2-bromobutane}$.

hints: Check the carbon bonded to Br in 2-bromobutane and list its four attached groups to decide if it is chiral.
Recall how to show 3D arrangement with solid wedge, hashed wedge and straight lines, and how the mirror image is formed by swapping two groups.
walkthrough:
Spot why this molecule is chiral**
Focus on C2, the $\text{CHBr}$ carbon. It is joined to four different groups: $\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Any carbon with four different groups is a chiral centre, so optical isomerism is possible.

Draw the first 3D isomer correctly**
Draw C2 in the centre. Put two bonds in the plane, for example $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, then put $\text{Br}$ on a solid wedge coming out toward you and $\text{H}$ on a hashed wedge going back. Label all four groups clearly.

Draw the mirror image as the second isomer**
Keep the same in plane groups but swap the wedge positions, so $\text{Br}$ is now on the hashed wedge and $\text{H}$ on the solid wedge. The two structures are mirror images and cannot be superimposed, so they are the pair of enantiomers.

Final answer: Pair of non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers) of 2-bromobutane centred on C2 bonded to $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{Br}$ and $\text{H}$, drawn with solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds, with two groups swapped between the two structures.

hints: Remember structural isomers have the same molecular formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br}$ but Br in a different position or on a different carbon skeleton.
Think of the two carbon skeletons possible for C4, straight chain butane and branched methylpropane.
Move Br to each unique position excluding the 2-bromobutane already given, to find three new structures.
walkthrough:
Keep the formula fixed**
You must stay as $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br}$. Do not change the numbers of C, H or Br. Only change connectivity. The given compound is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}$, so you need three different connectivities.

Use the straight chain in a new position**
Keep $\text{C-C-C-C}$ but move Br to the end: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$. This is 1-bromobutane, a position isomer.

Branch the chain and place Br in two ways**
Use the branched skeleton $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{3}$. Put Br on a primary carbon to get $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Br}$, and put Br on the central tertiary carbon to get $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{3}\text{CBr}$. These complete the three other structural isomers.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$ (1-bromobutane); $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Br}$ (1-bromo-2-methylpropane); $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{3}\text{CBr}$ (2-bromo-2-methylpropane)

hints: Expand $\text{(C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{)}_{3}\text{CBr}$ to see the longest chain through the C bonded to Br and count ethyl substituents.
walkthrough:
Unpack the condensed formula**
$\text{(C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{)}_{3}\text{CBr}$ means a central C bonded to Br and to three $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}$ groups. That central carbon is tertiary and very crowded.

Find the longest chain**
Take two ethyl groups end to end through the central C: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}\text{)BrCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. That is 5 carbons, so pentane. Br and an ethyl group are both on C3, giving $\text{3-bromo-3-ethylpentane}$.

hints: Consider the polarity of the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and which atom takes the bonding electrons when it breaks.
Recall what intermediate forms when a tertiary bromoalkane loses $\text{Br}^{-}$ and why it is relatively stable.
Think where the lone pair on $\text{OH}^{-}$ attacks and how to draw that curly arrow to the positive carbon.
walkthrough:
Show the bond breaking first**
Br is more electronegative than C, so show $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow starting on the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and pointing to Br, or just beyond it. This is heterolysis, both electrons go to Br to form $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Form the stable carbocation**
Losing $\text{Br}^{-}$ leaves $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{3}\text{C}^{+}$. This is a tertiary carbocation, stabilised by three electron donating ethyl groups, so it forms readily on its own without $\text{OH}^{-}$ helping at this stage.

Attack by the nucleophile**
Now show $\text{OH}^{-}$ with its lone pairs. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on O directly to the $\text{C}^{+}$ centre. The O-C bond forms to give the tertiary alcohol $\text{(C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{)}_{3}\text{COH}$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br to give $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{3}\text{C}^{+}$ + $\text{Br}^{-}$. Step 2: $\text{OH}^{-}$ attacks $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{3}\text{C}^{+}$ with curly arrow from O lone pair to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{3}\text{COH}$.

hints: Recall the name for replacement of Br by OH and whether the slow step involves one or two species for a tertiary halogenoalkane.
walkthrough:
Link observation to mechanism type**
Br is replaced by $\text{OH}$, so it is nucleophilic substitution. Because the rate determining step is loss of $\text{Br}^{-}$ to form the carbocation alone, it is unimolecular, $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$.
Final answer: $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ nucleophilic substitution

hints: Decide whether $\text{OH}^{-}$ should act as a nucleophile for substitution or as a base for elimination to give alkenes.
Recall the specific solvent and heating condition that favours elimination of HBr from a bromoalkane.
walkthrough:
Choose the role of hydroxide**
Aqueous $\text{OH}^{-}$ would substitute Br to give an alcohol. To remove HBr and make a $\text{C=C}$ double bond you need $\text{OH}^{-}$ to act as a base.

State the elimination conditions**
Use $\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{KOH}$ dissolved in ethanol, not water, and heat the mixture. Ethanolic hydroxide plus heat favours elimination to a mixture of alkenes.
Final answer: Sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide in ethanol / alcoholic, with heat

hints: Recall the term for loss of HBr to form a double bond, the opposite of addition.
walkthrough:
Name the bond change**
H and Br are lost from adjacent carbons and a $\text{C=C}$ bond forms. Loss of a small molecule to make an unsaturated product is elimination.

hints: Start from $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}$ and identify the two different adjacent carbons that can lose H to form $\text{C=C}$.
Recall why pent-2-ene can exist in two stereoisomeric forms while pent-1-ene cannot.
Remember skeletal formulae use lines for carbon skeleton with no C or H labels, showing the double bond position and cis versus trans arrangement.
walkthrough:
Find the two possible double bond positions**
Number the bromoalkane as C1 to C5 with Br on C2. Remove H from C1 to get the terminal alkene $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, pent-1-ene. Remove H from C3 to get the internal alkene $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, pent-2-ene.

Split pent-2-ene into cis and trans**
Pent-2-ene has two different groups on each $\text{C=C}$ carbon ($\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$ on one end, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ on the other), so restricted rotation gives cis and trans isomers. Pent-1-ene has two H atoms on C1 so shows no cis-trans isomerism.

Draw all three as skeletal formulae**
Draw zigzag lines: pent-1-ene has the double bond at the end of the chain. For cis-pent-2-ene draw the chain continuing on the same side of the double bond, for trans-pent-2-ene draw it continuing on opposite sides. Check each has 5 carbons total.

Final answer: Skeletal formulae of: pent-1-ene $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$; cis-pent-2-ene; trans-pent-2-ene, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ with correct cis and trans geometry about $\text{C=C}$.
